title: Della and Tock's Deep-Sea Discovery
markdown:
Della was a reef witch, not the cackling kind. Her cottage sat in the curve of a giant sleepy clam, pearly interior glowing from sunlight that filtered down. It smelled of sea breeze, warmth, and sometimes toasted seaweed crackers. Her hair was long emerald seaweed, swaying even without a current. Behind spectacles of polished pearl her eyes twinkled like a constellation of happy bioluminescent jellyfish.

Tock was a brass crab: shiny, clanky, little gears that went whirr-whirr-whirr when he thought hard, which was often. His shell gleamed like forgotten pirate treasure. His legs made a cheerful tap-tap-tap on coral. He found lost things — runaway pearls, misplaced hermit shells — and was about as brave as a barnacle that wanted to see the big waves: very brave, sometimes a little wobbly.

One sunny afternoon he rummaged near Anemone Acres for a pebble that had rolled from Della’s collection. “Where did it go?” Antennae twitching. Under swaying tentacles he found not a pebble but a small smooth pearly shell, pulsing with a warm inviting glow like a captured moonbeam taking a nap. He forgot the pebble. A sturdy brass claw. A scuttle home.

“Della! Look. Right by the Anemone Acres.” Happy clicks and clanks.

“Well, I’ll be pickled oysters.” Her spectacles slid. “This is not from around here. Ancient. Wonderfully mysterious.” Inside, faint silvery lines shimmered like moonlight on water: a symbol like a tangled string of stars, each connected by winding pathways.

She tapped her chin. “Great-great-great-great-aunt Merilda used to whisper about the Whispering Currents.”

Tock’s antennae nearly somersaulted. “Are they very noisy? Like shouting dolphins?”

Della giggled, silver bells underwater. “Not noisy. Rivers of water that carry secrets and forgotten tales. This shell feels like a piece of a map.” She pointed. “Pathways. Winding. Connecting. The old stories talked about land routes that were never one road — a web of paths, different wonders to different people.”

Tock tilted his shiny head. Gears thoughtful. “A web. Like a spiderweb, but for traders instead of flies.”

“Precisely. I think this points to one of those forgotten paths under the waves. We dive. First, supplies.” She packed a waterproof satchel: glowing sea-glow worms, a handful of sea-berry biscuits that tasted like sunshine and sweet berries.

Tock puffed his brass chest. Clank-squish. “Ready. Extra pressure. Murky water. I’m your crab.”

They went down past schools of fish like rainbow lightning, past giant swaying sea fans like delicate underwater trees. The satchel bumped Della’s hip. A sea-berry biscuit escaped and a passing wrasse stole it with excellent manners. Water darkened. The glow-worms woke in their jar, small patient moons. Currents that had been gentle began to guide, a friendly hand on the elbow. Then a strong swirl tried to shove them toward a dark spooky-looking shipwreck, ribs like teeth. “Hold on, Tock!” Della braced, hair streaming. Tock locked his extra grip on a stone and steered them off the danger, brass legs scraping a tune of protest. “Whoa. Close one.” His gears stuttered, then found their rhythm again.

They hung in the quieter water a moment, catching breath they did not strictly need. The pearly shell in Della’s palm pulsed warmer, as if it approved of not becoming wreck-furniture.

“This way.” Tock’s voice surprisingly strong. He pointed a sturdy claw at a shadowy opening in a large moss-covered rock. “The shell is humming stronger. I can feel it in my hinges.”

Della followed, kelp hair trailing like a silken scarf. And then they saw it: not a single clear road, a whole network of faint shimmering trails etched into the seabed, pathways woven from moonlight. They twisted and turned, connecting mysterious grottos and the silent ancient wrecks of old ships. A secret road made of the sea’s own magic. Della hovered, counting junctions the way Aunt Merilda had counted stories. Tock tapped one trail, then another, until the shell’s glow chose for them.

His keen eyes led her along that trail to a hidden alcove tucked behind a curtain of flowing seaweed. Nestled among soft velvety sea moss: a treasure chest, encrusted with shimmering pearls and sturdy barnacles, looking as if it had slept there for centuries. A little heave. A determined grunt. A mighty clanky effort from Tock. The lid complained, then gave.

Inside, no piles of gold coins, no sparkling jewels. Hundreds of beautiful iridescent shells, each unique, each humming a faint musical note. At the very bottom lay something more special: a small intricately carved wooden flute, wood that should have rotted and had not. Della picked it up gently. “Oh, Tock. A traveling musician, long ago. They carried their music the way others carried silk and spices along the old routes.”

She brought it to her lips and blew a soft sweet note. Instantly the shells hummed louder, individual notes joining a beautiful gentle symphony that filled the alcove. Light changed. The moss looked velvet-er. Tock scuttled, brass gleaming in the new melodic light, and did a little happy dance that turned into a clumsy flip. He landed with a muffled, slightly embarrassing bonk on the sandy floor. “Whoops.” Gears whirring with amusement.

Della laughed, and the laugh went into the music instead of over it. They did not need to say the ocean was connected. The trails were still shining when they looked back. They carefully closed the chest, leaving the shells to whisper to the deep quiet sea. Homeward they swam, hearts as full as a chest that had never wanted gold. The clam cottage waited with its seaweed-cracker smell and the missing pebble, which Tock found on the doorstep as if it had been embarrassed and come home by itself. His gears went whirr-whirr-whirr, already curious about the next lost thing, which was how most of their discoveries began.
characters: Della (a reef witch), Tock (a brass crab)
